title: Getting empty burned disc when calibrating boundary with CD-R
body:
@YukaiP Sorry for the slow reply, and thanks for trying disc-probe and posting the output.

Your screenshot shows a bug on our side. For CDs, disc-probe only ever suggests 1411 or 2822, so it kept sending you back to speeds you had already tried. At those speeds your drive keeps a constant linear speed (CLV), and in that mode disc-probe can't work out where each sector sits on the disc.

Many drives only switch to a constant spin (CAV) at their higher CD speeds. Could you try these in order, and stop at the first one that says CAV?

```
python -m discprobe timing --drive E: --media cd --speed 4234
python -m discprobe timing --drive E: --media cd --speed 5645
python -m discprobe timing --drive E: --media cd --speed 7056
```

If all three still say CLV, your SH-216DB probably never spins a CD at a constant rate, and disc-probe can't measure CD geometry with it yet. I'm fixing the speed suggestions so they stop repeating, and looking into whether a CLV drive can still be used. I'll post an update here.

title: Boundary Calibration fails validation despite hundreds of carefully placed points
body: I'm having trouble getting a valid result from Boundary Calibration. I carefully place points along the visible physical boundary on the calibration image. The number of points does not seem to solve the problem: I've tried both ~200 and over 450 points. The predicted boundary matches the manually marked points quite well near the inner radius, but progressively deviates toward the outer radius. If I place points starting from the outer edge and work toward the center, the opposite happens: the prediction matches the outer region but deviates toward the center. In other words, the prediction seems unable to match the entire boundary simultaneously. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Burn a Boundary Calibration target to a DVD+RW. 2. Take a photograph of the disc and load it into Boundary Calibration. 3. Carefully mark the visible boundary across the entire radial range. 4. Run the calibration. 5. Observe that the predicted boundary deviates progressively from the marked points in one part of the disc. 6. Try changing the distribution of marked points. The region where the prediction matches changes accordingly, but the full boundary still cannot be fitted. ## Error message With 423 manually placed points, the application reports: ``` [18:58:04] Calibration: Calculating parameters using all 423 curve points… [18:58:15] Calibration: Automatic validation did not pass. All 423 points and parameter candidates are preserved. Candidates can be applied after confirming the photographed match. The boundary segments do not match a single disc model. Check for misplaced points, photo rectification errors, or segments crossing another boundary. Candidates with different winding counts still fit these segments. Trace a longer, clear boundary at another radius and calculate again. ``` ## Expected behavior I would expect the calibration algorithm to use all marked points to find the best-fitting disc model, or clearly indicate which points or boundary segments are inconsistent with the model. ## Hardware and media - Drive: Pioneer DVR-218L - Firmware: 1.02 - Media: DVD+RW - Write speed: 4x - Application: DiscImageStudio v1.5.0+29b8cc1177c67a16b1ee5d2eb1a8c122f01cad17

title: Fine Calibration Issue
body: # Fine Calibration: predicted curve deviates significantly from manually traced boundary and marks valid points as outliers ## Description During Fine Calibration, the predicted curve can significantly deviate from the manually traced boundary, even when the boundary is clearly visible and has been carefully traced with a large number of points. In my test, I traced a highly irregular but clearly visible boundary using approximately 158 points. The points closely follow the actual photographed boundary, including its local bends and irregularities. However, the predicted curve does not follow the traced points. Instead, it appears excessively smoothed and deviates significantly from the actual trace, particularly near the inner and outer parts of the recording area. As a result, correctly placed points are highlighted as outliers, and the calibration reports very large errors. ## Observed results In the attached screenshot: - 158 points are retained. - `Fit cubic track pitch` is enabled. - Mean error: 1.399 mm. - Maximum error: 4.869 mm. - The predicted curve visibly diverges from the manually traced boundary. - Several correctly placed points are classified as large deviations. The actual boundary is clearly visible in the photograph and can be traced accurately. The discrepancy is between the traced points and the mathematical prediction, not necessarily the point placement. ## Expected behavior The fitting process should make effective use of all available traced points. In particular: 1. The predicted curve should represent the traced boundary as accurately as the selected mathematical model allows. 2. A large number of manually placed points should meaningfully constrain the fit. 3. The fitting process should not excessively smooth away local variations in the traced boundary. 4. Points should not be classified as outliers merely because the fitted model cannot reproduce local variations. 5. The application should make it possible to distinguish genuine tracing mistakes from limitations of the fitting model. It would also be useful to have an option to display the raw traced path without smoothing, alongside the fitted mathematical curve. ## Possible cause The fitting model may be too restrictive to represent the actual radial variation of the recorded track. The enabled cubic track pitch model uses a limited number of coefficients. It may be unable to reproduce local variations in the photographed boundary, causing the fitted curve to compromise between different radial regions. It is also worth investigating whether the fitting or visualization pipeline applies excessive smoothing or downsampling to the original points. ## Environment - DiscImageStudio v1.5.0 - Windows 10 x64 - Drive: Pioneer DVR-218L - Media: DVD+RW - Calibration stage: Fine Calibration - Traced points: approximately 158 - Cubic track pitch fitting: enabled

title: Two-level pattern invisible on a desktop drive (LG GH22NS40): recorded area uniform, only the recorded/unrecorded boundary visible — CD-R and DVD-R
body:
**摘要（中文）**：在台式 5.25 英寸刻录机 `HL-DT-ST DVDRAM GH22NS40` 上，CD-R 与 DVD-R 的双层图案均不可见。已排除速度（4×/16×）、介质批次与工具链：回读数据正确，**刻录区与未刻录区的边界清晰可见**，但刻录区内部没有任何图案。径向特征（同心环、刻录边界）可见，角向特征（半黑半白、文字、十字线）完全均匀。症状与 #292 / #242 / #295 一致，但本机是**台式机光驱**，不是薄型 USB 光驱。

---

## Environment

- **App**: DiscImageStudio CLI `v1.3.6` (`DiscImageStudio-CLI-v1.3.6-linux-x64.tar.gz`, SHA256 verified against the release `SHA256SUMS.txt`), self-contained, run on Arch Linux (kernel 7.2.8).
- **Drive**: `HL-DT-ST DVDRAM GH22NS40`, firmware `NL02`, SATA, **5.25" desktop drive** (serial `K5XA4J82909`). Reports MMC-2/3, DVD-R/-RW/-RAM, DVD+R/+RW, CD-R/RW, SAO/DAO, test write.
- **Burn tools**: `growisofs` (dvd+rw-tools) for DVD, `cdrecord 3.02a09` (cdrtools) `-dao` for CD. The app's Windows in-app burner is not used — this is the documented "export image + external burner" path.
- **Media**:
  - DVD-R 16× (generic, no MID read out), capacity 2 297 888 sectors.
  - CD-R 52× 700 MB (Multilaser). `cdrecord -atip` reports lead-in 97:27:18, lead-out 79:59:74 (359 849 sectors), "Medium Type B, low Beta category (B-)", short strategy type / phthalocyanine.

## What was produced

All images via the Linux CLI, then burned externally at the stated speed.

1. **CD-DA art, full disc** (concentric rings + large text), `cd-generate --sectors 359849`, burned `cdrecord dev=/dev/sr0 -dao speed=8 -audio` (and 4×, and 32× with a half-black/half-white image).
2. **DVD calibration card** (10 tone rings, solid black wedge, radial spokes, outer dashed band), `solve --total-sectors 2296437 --fill-sectors 2296416 --inner-radius-mm 24 --outer-radius-mm 58.04 --tone-dither 0.99`, burned `growisofs -Z ... -speed=4 -dvd-compat`.
3. **DVD text art** (`DISC` 175 pt, `2026` 100 pt, two smaller lines, thin ring), `--tone-dither 0`, burned at 4× and again at 16×.
4. **DVD radial half-fill** (only the inner half of the sectors written), `--fill-sectors 1148208`, burned at 4×.
5. **DVD angular half-black / half-white** (left half white, right half black), `--tone-dither 0`, burned at 16×.

Every burn completed with exit code 0 and no errors; every disc was closed and is readable.

## Observed

- **CD-R (all three speeds)**: data reads back correctly (`cdda2wav` returns the exact track length; the app reconstructs the art from the read-back WAV). On the disc, nothing but a ~1 mm ring near the hub; the rest of the data area is visually unchanged. Read-back shows ~12–14 % of samples muted to `0x00`, i.e. a marginal but readable burn.
- **DVD calibration card (4×)**: the ten tone rings look visible to a casual look, **but photo analysis of the data annulus gives a smooth monotonic radial profile** (116 → 200 → 160 across r = 100…340 px) with no ~20 px periodicity, and the solid black wedge region measures 158 — the *brightest* area of the disc. So the rings were most likely the generic diffraction of the data spiral, not the card.
- **DVD text art (4× and 16×)**: only a thin ring near the outer edge is visible; no letters at either speed.
- **DVD radial half-fill (4×)**: a **clear circular boundary** is visible at ~44 mm, exactly where the written region ends. This proves the drive and media do produce a visible mark/land-density difference at that scale.
- **DVD angular half-black/half-white (16×)**: the disc looks **uniformly burned** — no straight boundary, no spiral, no half-disc step.

## What this rules out

- **Speed**: 4× and 16× on DVD, 4×/8×/32× on CD — identical result.
- **Media batch**: two different media types (CD-R and DVD-R), different dyes, different wavelengths.
- **Toolchain / data correctness**: the app's own `simulate` reconstructs every image from the generated ISO, and the burned discs read back correctly.
- **Missing mark**: the recorded/unrecorded boundary is clearly visible, so the laser does modify the dye.
- **Rendering side / viewing angle**: verified under a point light at several angles; the uniform area stays uniform.
- **Wrong polarity**: the innermost calibration ring reads dark, i.e. the black level does render darker where it renders at all.

## Question

Issue #295 asks whether this is an expected limitation of **slim notebook-class drives** (write-strategy equalisation of mark/land density). This report is the same symptom on a **full-size 5.25" desktop drive**, which I believe has not been reported before, so it may narrow the cause:

1. Is this a known write-strategy equalisation behaviour that can affect desktop drives too, or is there a parameter we are missing?
2. Is there any media/drive combination known to work with this drive family (LG GH22NS40 / Renesas chipset)?
3. Would a different drive model be expected to change the result, before buying one?

Happy to run further tests on this exact hardware — the drive is available and the discs are sacrificial.

title: Two-level pattern invisible on a desktop drive (LG GH22NS40): recorded area uniform, only the recorded/unrecorded boundary visible — CD-R and DVD-R
body:
## Second drive tested — same result

I swapped the drive and repeated the exact same experiment.

- **Drive B**: `HL-DT-ST DVD-RAM GH22NS30`, firmware `2.00`, SATA, also a **5.25" desktop drive** (same HLDS family, one generation older than the GH22NS40).
- **Image**: identical `angular.iso` (left half pure white, right half pure black, `--tone-dither 0`, 2 296 416 sectors, r0 24 / r1 58.04 mm).
- **Burn**: `growisofs -Z /dev/sr0=angular.iso -speed=16 -dvd-compat` → exit 0, 16.0×, no errors, disc closed.

**Result: identical.** The disc looks uniformly burned — no straight boundary, no spiral, no half-disc step. Same as the GH22NS40 at 16×.

So this is not one specific drive model: two different HLDS drives (2008 and 2009 generations, different firmware) behave the same, on two different DVD-R batches.

## A pattern in the existing reports

Every report of this symptom I could find involves a **Hitachi-LG Data Storage** drive:

| Issue | Drive |
| --- | --- |
| this one | `HL-DT-ST DVDRAM GH22NS40` (desktop) |
| this one | `HL-DT-ST DVD-RAM GH22NS30` (desktop) |
| #295 | `HL-DT-ST DVDRAM GSA-T50L` (slim USB) |
| #242 | `LG HL-DT-ST DVDRAM GSA-H66N` (desktop) |
| #185 | `Transcend TS8XDVDS-K` (slim USB — these are usually HLDS OEM) |

That suggests the limiting factor may be the **HLDS write strategy**, which appears to equalise mark/land density inside the recorded area: the recorded/unrecorded boundary and the lead-out remain clearly visible, while the two-level pattern does not.

## Test that would settle it

A burn of the same ISO on a **non-HLDS drive** (Pioneer, ASUS, Lite-On, Plextor, or an older NEC/Optiarc). If the pattern appears there, the cause is confirmed as HLDS write strategy and the project could document a "known incompatible drive family" note. If it also fails on non-HLDS hardware, then the cause is broader than the drive family.

I still have both drives and sacrificial media and can run any further test you suggest.

title: Two-level pattern invisible on a desktop drive (LG GH22NS40): recorded area uniform, only the recorded/unrecorded boundary visible — CD-R and DVD-R
body:
## Following the HLDS hypothesis — next test planned

Both drives I tested report `HL-DT-ST` in INQUIRY, i.e. they are **Hitachi-LG Data Storage** units. Since every other report of this symptom also comes from HLDS hardware (#295 `GSA-T50L`, #242 `GSA-H66N`, #185 Transcend slim — very likely HLDS OEM), I am going to test the same ISO on a **non-HLDS** drive.

For anyone else following this, the INQUIRY vendor string tells you the real manufacturer, independent of the retail brand:

| INQUIRY vendor | Manufacturer | Expected to work? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HL-DT-ST` | HLDS (Hitachi-LG) | ❌ what failed in all reports so far |
| `TSSTcorp` | Toshiba-Samsung | untested |
| `PLDS` / `ATAPI` / `LITE-ON` | Lite-On | untested |
| `PIONEER` | Pioneer | untested |
| `Optiarc` / `SONY` | Sony-NEC | untested |
| `ASUS`, `LG`, `Verbatim`, `Teac`, `BenQ` | rebadged — may be any of the above | check the model |

Check with:

```bash
cdrecord -checkdrive dev=/dev/sr0 | grep -E 'Vendor_info|Identifikation'
```

## Test plan

1. Install a non-HLDS desktop drive (**Samsung SH-224DB**, `TSSTcorp`, is the cheapest and most common option here).
2. Verify the INQUIRY vendor string is not `HL-DT-ST`.
3. Burn the **same** `angular.iso` (left half white / right half black, `--tone-dither 0`, 2 296 416 sectors, r0 24 / r1 58.04 mm) with the same command: `growisofs -Z /dev/sr0=angular.iso -speed=16 -dvd-compat`.
4. Report whether the boundary is a straight diameter, a spiral, or absent.

I will post the result here, including photos, so the HLDS hypothesis is either confirmed or refuted with hardware evidence.

If the maintainer has a specific drive family or firmware known to produce visible two-level art, that would save a purchase — otherwise I will report back with the TSST result.

title: Two-level pattern invisible on a desktop drive (LG GH22NS40): recorded area uniform, only the recorded/unrecorded boundary visible — CD-R and DVD-R
body:
## The pattern *is* written — it is rotated. Geometry sweep results

Following the earlier comments, I found a way to separate "no contrast" from "wrong geometry": the half-black/half-white image does show structure if you look closely — but the dividing line arrives as a **spiral**, not as a straight diameter. So the two-level pattern is being recorded; it is rotated by an angular error that accumulates with radius.

That makes the drift measurable: the distance between consecutive turns of that spiral is the drift per revolution.

### Method

Same image (`angular.png`, left half pure white / right half pure black), same command, same drive (`GH22NS30`), same media, `--tone-dither 0`, burned at 16×. Only `--outer-radius-mm` changes, always with `--total-sectors 2297888` (the disc's own `Track Size`) and `--fill-sectors 2297824`.

Ring count is measured over the **first 10 mm** from the inner data edge, with a steel rule laid on the disc.

| `--outer-radius-mm` | rings per 10 mm | implied spacing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 58.040 | 18 | 0.56 mm |
| 58.008 | 16 | 0.63 mm |
| **57.800** | **6** | **1.67 mm** |

Photos of the first two measurements (rule in frame, same disc surface):

![r1 = 58.040 — 18 rings per 10 mm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ghpo/discimagestudio-evidence/main/midia-1medicao.jpg)

![r1 = 58.008 — 16 rings per 10 mm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ghpo/discimagestudio-evidence/main/midia-2medicao.jpg)

### The part that does not fit

At `r1 = 57.800` the first centimetre improves a lot (18 → 6 rings), **but the spacing keeps shrinking with radius**: after that first centimetre the rings become progressively finer until there are more than 70 of them and a phone camera can no longer resolve them.

For a constant pitch error the spacing would be **constant** across the radius. For a linear pitch coefficient (`--pitch-linear a1`) it would vary smoothly. Fitting the observed 5–10× change in spacing to `pitch(r) = p0 (1 + a1 x)` requires `a1 ≈ -5`, i.e. a negative track pitch — physically impossible.

So the residual is **not** a radius or pitch error that the documented parameters can express. What remains is the mapping between sector number and physical angle: the model assumes the ideal CLV relationship, and this drive appears to deviate from it in a way that varies with radius.

### Questions

1. Is there any CLI parameter (or a value the GUI's fine calibration produces) that compensates for a sector→angle mapping deviation rather than a radius/pitch deviation?
2. Does the GUI's spoke calibration measure exactly this — and would its result be usable from the CLI via `--pitch-*`? If so, which coefficient carries the angular term?
3. If this is a known drive limitation, is there a list of drives known to work? Both drives here are HLDS (`GH22NS40`, `GH22NS30`), consistent with the pattern noted earlier.

For completeness: with the unmodified preset geometry (`--total-sectors 2296437`, `r1 = 58.04`) the same image produced a disc that looked completely uniform, and the drift only became visible as a measurable spiral after switching to the disc's real sector count. That step alone may be worth documenting.

Happy to run more experiments — both drives and sacrificial media are still available. A flatbed scan of the disc is also possible if that would help quantify the spacing profile.
